uncited: It builds on [Spherical Panoramic Gaussian Splatting (SPaGS)](3042-spherical-panoramic-gaussian-splatting-spags.md).
**Inputs:** 3D Gaussian splat parameters (mean $\mathbf{m}$, covariance $\Sigma$) in camera space; spherical camera projection parameters (equirectangular image dimensions $W \times H$).
**Outputs:** Axis-aligned 2D bounding box $(p_{x,\min}, p_{y,\min}, p_{x,\max}, p_{y,\max})$ on the equirectangular image plane.

*   **Tangent Space Basis:** Three normalized vectors $\hat{\mathbf{t}}$ (tangent), $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ (bitangent), $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ (normal) representing the local x, y, z axes of the tangent space.
*   **Tangent Space Bounding Box:** Four floats $(t_{x,\min}, t_{x,\max}, t_{y,\min}, t_{y,\max})$ defining the rectangle in the tangent plane $z=1$.
*   **Camera Space Coordinates:** Derived from tangent coordinates using transformation matrix.
For each splat, compute the normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ from the covariance matrix.
The origin of the tangent space is the camera space origin.
Calculate the minimum and maximum $p_y$ (latitude) and $p_x$ (longitude) on the equirectangular plane.

If the projected bounding box covers the north or south pole (determined by checking if the latitude range includes $\pm \pi/2$), calculate $p_{y,\min}$ and $p_{y,\max}$ similarly for the projection center on the respective sphere.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ per splat, as it involves a fixed number of matrix operations and trigonometric functions.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ per splat, storing only the bounding box coordinates.
*   **Strengths:** Handles spherical projection distortion accurately; numerically stable at poles; avoids loose approximations of 3D bounding box projections.
*   **When to use:** Real-time rendering of 3D Gaussians on spherical panoramas (e.g., VR, 360° video) where standard affine rasterization fails due to non-linear projection.

The claim describes the calculation of the tangent vector t̂ as the normalized cross product of a reference vector r_ref and the normal vector n̂, and the bitangent vector b̂ as the cross product of n̂ and t̂. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states that 'the reference vector is defined as r_ref, except when the mean of the splat lies on the vector of the two poles, in which case we use r_ref to avoid singularity' (note: the text likely implies a different vector for poles, but the general definition for non-pole cases uses r_ref). It further defines t̂, b̂, and n̂ as normalized tangent, bitangent, and normal vectors. In standard tangent space construction (and implied by the context of defining an orthonormal basis for the tangent plane), t̂ is derived from the cross product of the reference and normal vectors to ensure orthogonality, and b̂ is derived from n̂ × t̂ to complete the right-handed system. The evidence supports the components and the general method described in the claim.
